transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-08 15:30 UTC  | Duration: 42m | Recording link: (redacted)
Attendees: Sanjay Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Alex Moreno (Head of ML, Harbinger), Priya Singh (Platform Eng), Jordan Lee (CTO)

Summary:
Short intake to understand Harbinger's reserved GPU needs, isolation constraints and burst model. Customer is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private; leaning toward Dedicated with strict tenant isolation but wants a burst/fallback strategy to hosted. Discussed benchmarking, model size/throughput, KV cache concerns and encryption/KMS. Agreed next steps for pricing + bench run.

00:00:08 - Speaker 1 (Sanjay): Hey thanks everyone for carving out time. quick intros? i'm sanjay, account lead, and maya's our solutions engineer who will run the bench.
00:00:20 - Speaker 2 (Alex): yeah alex here, head of ml at harbinger. thanks for squeezing us in. we wanted to get upfront about capacity commitments—our app is latency sensitive and we have compliance constraints.
00:00:33 - Speaker 3 (Priya): priya platform engineering, i'll own the infra side and networking.
00:00:38 - Speaker 4 (Jordan): jordan, cto. high level: we need predictability in cost and capacity for Q4.
00:00:47 - Speaker 1 (Sanjay): great. quick agenda: current stack, peak patterns, isolation needs, burst/fallback, security, pilot next steps. sound good?
00:00:56 - Speaker 2 (Alex): yep.

00:01:40 - Maya: can you paint your current stack and where inference runs today?
00:01:46 - Alex: sure. we're running a mix. prod is kubernetes on-prem for now, 8xA100 in two racks, using Triton for inference and a homegrown sharding layer called "harp-sched". we've also been experimenting with smaller models in the cloud but it's fragmented.
00:02:05 - Priya: our platform uses k8s with custom device plugin. we do prewarm pools with a cronjob but that's brittle.
00:02:15 - Maya: okay do you already have containerized model packages and a KV cache?
00:02:20 - Alex: yes containerized, the checkpoint sits in our internal artifact repo. we use a prefix cache—kv cache—but sometimes the KKV cache evicts and causes cold-start latency spikes.
00:02:34 - Maya: gotcha, we often see that; Redwood has prefix caching and warm-pool features which help. question for you: what's a typical request distribution, token lengths, and p95 latency targets?
00:02:46 - Alex: average request 25 tokens, p95 end-to-end latency needs to be under 250ms for our main flow. We can accept a 400-500ms tail for internal batch ops.
00:02:58 - Jordan: and we expect 2x traffic spikes during product releases, so we want burst capability that doesn't blow the budget.

00:04:10 - Maya: are you evaluating hosted as the fallback or private? how strict is your tenancy isolation requirement?
00:04:18 - Alex: tenancy is important—customer data can't be co-mingled with other tenants. we want isolated capacity, ideally single-tenant GPUs or strong tenant separation at the instance level.
00:04:30 - Priya: we also have encryption-at-rest and KMS policies, key rotation requirements, and SS0 via our IdP (saml).
00:04:40 - Maya: okay, sounds like Redwood Dedicated with VPC peering and dedicated node pools is a fit. Private (on-prem) is an option but heavier. Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools that are single-tenant and can be configured with customer-managed KMS for model keys.
00:04:55 - Alex: quick question — in the Dedicated offering, is the control plane multi-tenant? we need audit logs & separation.
00:05:03 - Sanjay: yes the control plane is shared, but we provide per-customer RBAC, audit logs and exportable S3 audit streams. for higher compliance we can discuss a Private deployment or a Dedicated with a dedicated control plane — that's on term negotiation.

00:06:12 - Speaker 1 (Alex): pricing? we need committed baseline but want the option to burst. what does that look like?
00:06:20 - Sanjay: typically there's a reserved commit for baseline capacity and then a burst pricing tier for excess usage. you can pre-warm extra nodes as part of burst pools. pricing tiers depend on GPU class, and commitment length (monthly vs annual). we'll share a sample price sheet.
00:06:40 - Jordan: how does prewarm work — is it billed while prewarmed? we don't want to pay full price for idle prewarmed GPUs.
00:06:48 - Maya: good point. Redwood has a hot-pool prewarm option with a reduced prewarm fee and then a full runtime charge when serving. you can configure prewarm timeouts. we also offer autoscale with warm-signal heuristics so the runtime keeps KV caches warmed for common prefixes.

00:07:35 - Priya: networking: we need VPC peering, private egress, and the ability to restrict egress IPs. can you support static egress?
00:07:44 - Maya: yes VPC peering and static egress IPs are supported in Dedicated and Private offerings. we'll share the network diagram. note: if you use Hosted fallback, egress paths differ unless you do a dedicated region.

00:08:50 - Alex: latency question. our app is very latency sensitive. we measured token throughput on A100 and saw kv cache misses push us to 700-800ms occasionally. How do you guarantee tails?
00:09:01 - Maya: we set latency SLOs per route; the runtime does continuous batching but also has fast-paths for short sequences. prewarming the KV cache and using smaller quantized variants helps. Also, you can pin hot routes to reserved instances to reduce variability.
00:09:20 - Alex: ok, if we pin to dedicated nodes, what's the isolation at a CUDA-context level? we need to ensure model weights aren't paged to other tenants' memory.
00:09:31 - Maya: dedicated GPU nodes are isolated at the instance level — separate processes and memory. the only shared pieces are the control plane and monitoring agents, and we encrypt model artifacts at rest. for extra guarantees there's a private on-prem package.

00:11:00 - Jordan: security — SOC 2, ISO, pen test reports, SSO, RBAC, KMS. can we get those docs?
00:11:07 - Sanjay: yes we'll send SOC 2 report, pen test summary, and SAML SSO docs. for KMS we support AWS KMS and external HSMs via customer-managed keys.

00:12:22 - Alex: about the bench — we want an apples-to-apples check. our model is a 13B transformer, sparsified quantized candidate, serves both chat and single-turn generation. we'd like a run that mimics our traffic shape with spikes.
00:12:37 - Maya: perfect. we'll do a 2-hour bench with your checkpoint, sample prompt set, and a spike pattern. we'll measure p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1k tokens, and demonstrate recovery from cold-starts.
00:12:49 - Alex: do you let us run the bench in our VPC or do we run against dedicated infra hosted by you?
00:12:56 - Maya: both approaches possible. often for initial perf we run on Redwood Dedicated infra in our region with a shared bench harness; for final validation we can run in your VPC in Private mode.

00:14:10 - Priya: integration points — what do we need to provide for the bench? checkpoint, a small request driver, and some sample telemetry endpoints?
00:14:20 - Maya: yes: model tarball or s3 path, sample prompt file (CSV), tokenization script if custom, concurrency profile, and your target SLOs. also network access rules for our bench agent if we run from your VPC.

00:15:05 - Speaker 5 (Alex, misattributed at times): we've had trouble with prewarm when we deploy new model versions — cold starts kill us. is there a workflow to do canary rollouts with warm cache?
00:15:18 - Maya: yes, Redwood supports canary + canary prewarm: you can keep a percentage of traffic on old model while prewarming the new weights in the hot pool. we also support automatic fallback to a smaller variant if the new model exceeds latency thresholds.

00:17:00 - Alex: curious about quantization — we use int8 and some FP16 in internal tests. do you have quantized kernels for our model?
00:17:08 - Maya: we have optimized kernels for most Transformer variants and quantization modes; our compiler chooses kernels for sequence length and batch. sometimes names get fuzzy in transcription, but we can share our kernel matrix and expected performance for 13B int8.

00:18:40 - Jordan: operationally, who runs the Dedicated infra — you or a partner? what happens during regional outages?
00:18:50 - Sanjay: Redwood operates dedicated pools in the cloud with isolation. for outages we have smart routing and fallback policies to other regions or to hosted-compatible variants; you can also configure multi-region redundancy with reservations.

00:20:12 - Priya: audit trail question — we need verifiable logs for every inference request and model version for compliance. is that feasible?
00:20:21 - Maya: yes we can export per-request metadata to your S3, include model version, route, tokens, and latencies. you can configure retention policies. sensitive payloads can be redacted at ingestion or kept in your VPC for Private deployments.

00:22:05 - Alex: ok timeline: we need something in Q4. pilot in October ideally. is that doable?
00:22:12 - Sanjay: yes if we start the bench this month and agree reserved baseline it's feasible. typical pilot runs 2-4 weeks including bench, integration and an SLA smoke test.

00:25:30 - (brief side discussion about legal terms and data residency)
00:26:05 - Jordan: contracting — we'd need data residency in us-east and an addendum for insurance around customer data.
00:26:13 - Sanjay: noted, we'll loop legal.

00:27:45 - (Audio glitch for 10s, partial words)
00:27:56 - Alex: sorry lost you — could you repeat the prewarm billing model?
00:28:02 - Maya: sure — there's a reduced prewarm hourly fee and a normal usage per-second rate when serving; for long-running prewarmed nodes we can negotiate a lower reserved hourly price.

00:29:20 - Priya: what's the SLA on latency and availability for Dedicated?
00:29:27 - Sanjay: Dedicated has an availability SLA for the reserved pool (99.9+ depending on tier). latency SLOs are per-route and we publish historical latency distributions in the console for your org.

00:31:10 - Alex: any pitfalls you've seen in migrating from on-prem k8s to a dedicated cloud pool?
00:31:18 - Maya: common ones: tokenization differences, hidden assumptions about batch sizes, and KV cache hotkey patterns. also networking and egress IPs. We recommend a staged migration: bench, small pilot, then ramp with canaries.

00:33:05 - Jordan: do you support bring-your-own-license for certain kernels or optimizations?
00:33:12 - Maya: some customers bring optimized kernels; we have an onboarding path but we need to audit kernel safety. usually the compiler handles kernel selection.

00:34:40 - Alex: okay let's recap next steps.
00:34:45 - Sanjay: recap: 1) Maya to draft bench plan, 2) Sanjay to send pricing + sample reservation SLO doc, 3) Harbinger to deliver model artifact and prompt set, 4) schedule bench 2-hour slot next week, 5) send SOC2 and KMS docs.
00:35:05 - Alex: that's right. also please include an example fallback policy and how billing looks during a burst.
00:35:16 - Maya: we'll include an example burst policy with cost simulations.

00:36:30 - (closing)
00:36:35 - Jordan: thanks everyone, helpful call. we'll review and aim to provide artifacts by Friday.
00:36:43 - Sanjay: thanks all. we'll follow up in email with calendar invites for bench and the docs.
